---
title: "Elements are objects"
---

Your starter project is running and the page says `Hello World!`. One line in
`src/index.ts` added that exclamation mark, and that line begins with
`document.getElementById`. The call hands your program an **object**, and that
word follows you through the rest of the book. This chapter shows you what the
object is and what you can do with it.

## Two variables, one heading {#sec-elements-are-objects-experiment}

Open the project from the previous chapter and replace everything in
`src/index.ts` with these lines:

```ts
const heading = document.getElementById('helloWorldHeader') as HTMLHeadingElement;
const sameHeading = document.getElementById('helloWorldHeader') as HTMLHeadingElement;

heading.textContent = 'Two variables, one heading';

console.log(sameHeading.textContent);
```

Two calls, two variables. The program writes text through the first variable
and reads text back through the second one. Write your prediction on paper
before you run anything: what will the console line show?

Start the app with `npm start` and open the address it prints. Then open the
browser's developer tools with **F12** (`Cmd`+`Option`+`I` on a Mac) and click
the **Console** tab. Every browser has one.

The console shows `Two variables, one heading`. That is the text you never
wrote through `sameHeading`.

## The elements panel shows the same page {#sec-elements-are-objects-devtools}

Stay in the developer tools and switch to the **Elements** tab (Firefox calls
it **Inspector**). It shows your page as HTML, and moving the mouse over a row
highlights that piece of the page. Double-click the text inside the `<h1>`
row, type your own words, and press Enter. The heading on the page changes
while you type.

Now press F5 to reload. Your typing is gone and the heading reads
`Two variables, one heading` again. The elements panel never touched a file on
your disk. It changed what the browser is holding in memory at this moment,
and the page followed along, because the panel and the page show the same
thing from two sides.

## A page is a tree {#sec-elements-are-objects-tree}

HTML describes a page with **tags**. Here is a small page, shorter than the
one in your project:

```html
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>Hello</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1 id="helloWorldHeader">Hello World</h1>
    <p>A page is a tree.</p>
    <ul>
      <li>First item</li>
      <li>Second item</li>
    </ul>
  </body>
</html>
```

`<h1>` opens a heading and `</h1>` closes it again. The opening tag, the
closing tag, and everything between them are one **element**. Inside an
opening tag you can write **attributes**, extra information in the form
`name="value"`. The heading carries one: `id="helloWorldHeader"` gives that
single element a name, and a name is what you need to find it again from
TypeScript.

Elements sit inside other elements. Both `<li>` elements sit inside the
`<ul>`. That `<ul>` sits inside `<body>`, and `<body>` sits inside `<html>`.
Nesting like that turns a page into a tree.

![The small page above, drawn as a tree. Every element hangs somewhere below `document`.](images/dom-tree.svg){width=420}

## The DOM {#sec-elements-are-objects-dom}

While the browser reads your HTML, it builds one object for every element it
finds and hangs those objects into the tree from the picture. The whole set is
called the **DOM**, short for **Document Object Model**: the browser's objects
for the elements of your page.

An **object** is a thing in your program that carries named values, and each
named value is a **property**. You have used two properties of the heading
object already. `textContent` is the text inside the element, and `id` is the
name from the HTML attribute. Reading a property looks like reading a
variable, and writing to one looks like an assignment:

```ts
console.log(heading.id); // helloWorldHeader
heading.textContent = 'Changed from TypeScript';
```

A tree needs a root, and the root of the DOM is `document`, the object for the
whole page. Every search for an element starts there, which is why your line
starts with `document.getElementById`.

::: {.callout-note}
## What `as HTMLHeadingElement` is doing there

`document.getElementById` can return any element, so TypeScript does not know
that this one is a heading. The `as HTMLHeadingElement` part tells TypeScript
what kind of element it is. Copy it for now, the chapter on types for elements
explains it.
:::

The starter's original line used `innerText` instead of `textContent`. The two
are cousins: `innerText` asks what a reader sees on screen, `textContent`
gives you the text as it stands in the tree. This course writes `textContent`
everywhere, and you can leave the cousin alone.

## One element, many variables {#sec-elements-are-objects-identity}

`getElementById` never creates a heading. It searches the tree for an element
with that `id` and hands back a **reference** to the object it found. Two
calls with the same `id` find the same object, so both variables end up
pointing at it. One heading, two names for it.

You met that idea last year with arrays. An array variable holds an arrow to
the array instead of the array itself, so two variables can point at one array
and a change through either one shows up in both. Element variables behave the
same way. In the experiment at the top of this chapter,
`heading.textContent = ...` followed the arrow and changed the one heading
object that exists, and `sameHeading.textContent` followed a second arrow to
that same object and read the new text.

**Try it.** Add a third variable with a third `getElementById` call and log
its `textContent` as well. Both logs show the same text, and the page still
has exactly one heading.

## Looking things up on MDN {#sec-elements-are-objects-mdn}

`textContent` and `id` are two properties out of a long list, and this book
never prints that list. The people who build the browsers keep it for you on
MDN Web Docs, the reference for everything a browser can do.

Open the [MDN page for `textContent`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Node/textContent)
and see how such a page is built. It starts with one sentence saying what the
property is, then a "Value" section saying what you get, then examples. Later
chapters send you to MDN on purpose, with questions you answer before you can
finish the exercise. Getting comfortable with these pages now makes those
chapters short.

## Exercise: hello again {#sec-elements-are-objects-exercise}

Build a small page that greets you, prints today's date, and counts clicks.

1. Create a new app from the
   [vite-ts-starter](https://github.com/Teaching-HTL-Leonding/vite-ts-starter)
   template and run `npm install`. Start it with `npm start`. The page shows
   `Hello World!`.

2. Open `index.html` and add three lines below the `<h1>`:

   ```html
   <h2 id="myName">Your name</h2>
   <p id="today">Today</p>
   <button id="clickMe" type="button" onclick="count()">Click me</button>
   ```

   Reload the page. You see the placeholder texts and a button. Clicking it
   does nothing yet and the console reports that `count` is not defined.

3. Open `src/index.ts`, delete what the starter wrote there, and put your own
   name into the second heading. Use the same shape as in the experiment:
   fetch the element by its `id` into a `const`, then set its `textContent`.
   The element with the `id` `myName` is an `HTMLHeadingElement`, so the `as`
   part stays the same as well. After the reload the page greets you by name.

4. Below that, write today's date into the paragraph. The browser knows the
   date, and this expression gives it to you as a string in the local format:

   ```ts
   new Date().toLocaleDateString()
   ```

   Fetch the paragraph with the `id` `today` (its type is
   `HTMLParagraphElement`) and set its `textContent` to a sentence that
   contains that date. Reload and check that the date is right.

5. Now the button. The `onclick` attribute you typed in step 2 needs a
   function named `count` that belongs to the whole page, and a function in
   `src/index.ts` is not that. The `<script type="module">` tag at the bottom
   of `index.html` loads your TypeScript as a **module**, and everything
   declared in a module stays inside that module. So the counter goes into a
   plain `<script>` tag instead. Add this block right above the
   `<script type="module">` line in `index.html`:

   ```html
   <script>
   let clicks = 0;

   function count() {
     clicks = clicks + 1;
     const button = document.getElementById('clickMe');
     button.textContent = `Clicks: ${clicks}`;
   }
   </script>
   ```

   Click the button three times. It reads `Clicks: 3`.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The script block is ugly on purpose

That `<script>` block is JavaScript written straight into your HTML file,
outside every tool you have. TypeScript never sees it, and VS Code may even
underline `count` as unused, because the checker does not look inside HTML
attributes. Keep it for one chapter anyway, because it gets your button
working today. The next chapter builds the same button without any such
block, from `src/index.ts` alone.
:::

Look at where the texts on your page come from. The `<h1>` shows what you
typed into `index.html`. The second heading and the paragraph get their text
from TypeScript while the page loads, and the button rewrites its own text on
every click. Those last two do the same thing in the end, setting
`textContent` on an element object.
